title: Russia Passes Law to Regulate Crypto Exchanges, Keeps Payment Ban in Place
dek: Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a law establishing exchange licensing requirements and regulating digital currencies, while maintaining a prohibition on using crypto as payment within Russia. The law caps retail investor trading at 300,000 rubles ($3,700) annually, though qualified investors face no limits.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: Russia formalized crypto exchange regulation while preserving its 2022 payment prohibition, despite Putin's 2024 public statements praising Bitcoin's utility.
bottom_line: Russia has formalized exchange oversight while preserving its payment ban, creating a regulated trading environment without crypto-as-money functionality. Watch whether the qualified investor exemption and foreign-trade carve-out become de facto channels for broader crypto use, and whether the "most liquid cryptocurrency" definition expands or contracts in implementation.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a law establishing a formal regulatory framework for digital currencies and digital rights in the country, according to Bitcoin Magazine. The legislation permits only registered entities to operate as exchanges and creates a two-tier trading structure tied to investor qualification status.

Retail investors are now capped at 300,000 rubles, approximately $3,700, per year for trading what the law defines as "most liquid cryptocurrencies." Qualified investors face no restrictions on trading volume. The new rules establish exchange licensing as a formal requirement, shifting Russia's approach from de facto prohibition toward managed participation.

The law explicitly prohibits digital currencies and digital rights from functioning as a means of payment or legal tender within Russia, per Bitcoin Magazine. This payment ban has been in place since 2022. However, the law includes a specific carve-out: Russians engaged in foreign trade or crypto mining may use digital currencies to settle payments under contracts with non-residents, the outlet reported.

The move creates a stated tension with public messaging from the Russian leadership. In 2024, Putin said, "For example, Bitcoin, who can ban it? Nobody," and highlighted Russia's competitive advantages in Bitcoin mining due to access to cheap energy, according to Bitcoin Magazine. Yet the new law maintains the payment restriction that predates those comments and introduces a retail trading cap.

The scope of which cryptocurrencies fall under "most liquid" remains undefined in the available regulatory reporting, leaving ambiguity about which assets retail participants may access under the 300,000-ruble threshold.
